subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Availability Heuristic: If It's Memorable, It's Common
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Availability Heuristic: If It's Memorable, It's Common.

hook.text: Which kills more people: shark attacks or falling coconuts? Coconuts, by a factor of 15. You guessed sharks.

buildup.text: The availability heuristic: we judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind.

discovery.text: Dramatic, emotional, or recent events are easiest to recall — so we overestimate their frequency.

twist.text: Media amplifies this. Plane crashes are rare but vivid. Car deaths are common but boring. We fear the wrong one.

climax.text: Availability shapes policy: billions spent on terrorism prevention, far less on heart disease — the actual top killer.

punchline.text: Memorable isn't the same as common. Your brain confuses them.

quiz.question: What does the availability heuristic cause us to do?
options: Overestimate the frequency of vivid, memorable events

details.summary: The availability heuristic judges the frequency or probability of events by how easily examples come to mind. Dramatic plane crashes feel more dangerous than car accidents because they are more memorable, not more common.
details.whyItMatters: This heuristic distorts risk assessment, policy preferences, and personal decisions by making vivid events seem far more likely than they are.
takeaways: Ease of recall substitutes for actual frequency data
Media coverage amplifies availability of dramatic events
Base rates provide the necessary correction

faq.question: Why do people fear flying more than driving despite lower crash rates?
faq.answer: Plane crashes receive massive media coverage, making them vivid and easy to recall. Car accidents are common but rarely make national news. The availability heuristic mistakes memorability for probability.

faq.question: How can you correct for the availability heuristic when assessing risk?
faq.answer: Look up actual statistics rather than trusting your intuitive sense of frequency. Ask whether your estimate is based on data or on how easily you can picture a vivid example.
